content: On the eve of James Buchanan's inauguration as President of the United States in February 1857, an outbreak of illness occurred at the National Hotel in Washington, D.C., which was the largest and most popular hotel in the city at the time, particularly among Southerners. Buchanan himself fell ill, as did several of his close friends and associates. This led to speculation and conspiracy theories suggesting that the illness, later referred to as National Hotel Disease, might have been caused by poison deliberately introduced into the hotel's food supply by abolitionists who were angered by Buchanan's pro-slavery stance and his victory over Republican John C. Frémont in the election. Other theories posited that pro-slavery partisans might have been responsible, as Vice President John C. Breckinridge, a pro-slavery Southerner, would have assumed the presidency if Buchanan had died. However, the more plausible explanation is that the illness was caused by unsanitary conditions in Washington, D.C., exacerbated by the harsh winter that year. The freezing temperatures caused the hotel's plumbing to fail, leading to a sewage backup that contaminated the kitchen. The bacterial strain or strains involved in the outbreak were likely highly virulent, as many of the affected guests remained ill for months or even years, and several ultimately died from the disease. Buchanan himself was bedridden for the first six weeks of his presidency. Among those who succumbed to the illness were Mississippi Congressman John Quitman and Pennsylvania Congressman John Gallagher Montgomery. Other prominent figures, such as Massachusetts Congressman Jonathan Edwards Field and New Hampshire Senator John Parker Hale, also contracted the disease and suffered long-term effects for years afterward.
